sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Maastricht's street-parking policy is tied to a 2003 agreement with Q-Park: street tariffs must be equal to or higher than those in nearby Q-Park garages, so that long-stay visitors are steered into garages and street spaces stay free for short stays and permit holders [0]. The college raised street tariffs by 15 percent from 1 January 2024, to 3.50 euros an hour in the city centre and 7.80 euros for a day ticket, citing the agreement, national tariffs and parking income about 1 million euros below budget in 2022 [1]. For 2025 it indexed them by 3.3 percent [2]. For 2026 the college decided on 16 September 2025 to send the tariffs to the council for 4 November 2025, a 2.1 percent general index at that date; we did not find the vote [4]. The page we read in October 2026 shows 3.70 euros an hour in the high-tariff zone, 1.90 in the low-tariff zone and 8.30 for a day ticket [5], paid on shop-opening days: 08:00 to 18:00 on most days, to 21:00 on Thursday and 12:00 to 18:00 on Sunday [6].

Permits are restricted: since 1 January 2022 residents of the Binnenstad can have at most one permit and only if they have no private parking [11], at 30.08 euros a month in the Binnenstad [10]. From 1 January 2025 the city centre is a zero-emission zone for city logistics; passenger cars are not covered [13]. The 'autoluw Wyck' pilot started on 5 January 2026 for a year, barring cars from part of Wycker Brugstraat in the evenings and at weekends and pointing drivers to nearby garages [12].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: We found no news on new, closed or refurbished garages. The changes are in park and ride and in busy-day measures. P+R Maastricht Noord (516 spaces) is free to park, with the bus costing 1.28 euros per trip with OVpay [8], and on 12 October 2026 Maastricht Bereikbaar announced that the ticket machine there disappears after 31 December 2026, so travellers will check in and out with OVpay [9]. On especially busy days, such as holidays and events like Magisch Maastricht, the city, Maastricht Bereikbaar and Q-Park run 'Topdagen Plus' measures with extra traffic regulators, signs showing free garage spaces and extra enforcement [16]. For drivers from Belgium the advice is to use Fort Willem at 8.30 euros a day or Frontenpark, noting that garages near the centre often fill up quickly at weekends [17]. Maastricht has about 500 public charging posts and expects to double the number of charge points to about 2,000 by 2030 [15].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Q-Park runs the main garages, and their tariffs are set by the municipality under the 2003 agreement, indexed each year by the September consumer price index since 2015, with equal tariffs per ring: Vrijthof as ring 0, the core shopping area ring 1, the centre ring 2 and Park & Walk ring 3 [3]. The 2026 flyer lists Vrijthof at 1.50 euros per 16 minutes and 35 euros a day, Frontenpark and several others at 1.50 euros per 32 minutes and 18 euros a day, and Fort Willem at 8.30 euros a day [7]. Q-Park's pages give capacities of 1,308 spaces at Frontenpark, 1,089 at Mosae Forum, 449 at Plein 1992 and 447 at Vrijthof [14].

Our data cover only two park-and-ride sites, P+R Station (340 spaces) and Meerssenerweg (66), measured for 61 days since 22 August 2026, which together averaged about 24% on weekdays and 26% at weekends. P+R Station never exceeded 54%, while the small Meerssenerweg site averaged 35% and reached full in a single Saturday-morning reading. We have no readings for the city-centre garages, so these figures say nothing about the garages the tariff policy is built around.
